title: The Guy Next Door
author: LokkeeVerse
content:
The afternoon sun hung over the quiet suburban street, turning the pavement silver with heat. From her kitchen window, Lila Harper watched a moving truck pull into the driveway next door.

She had lived in the same house for three years. She knew which neighbor watered their flowers before breakfast, which couple argued behind closed curtains, and which dog barked at passing cars as if protecting the entire street.

Her neighborhood was predictable.

Then the new neighbor stepped out of the truck.

He was tall, broad-shouldered, and dressed in nothing but dark shorts. His deep brown skin glistened beneath the afternoon sun as he lifted a heavy box from the truck and carried it toward his front door without apparent effort.

Lila forgot about her coffee.

She had promised herself that this year would be different. No more emotionally unavailable men. No more confusing attraction with compatibility. No more letting a handsome face disrupt her carefully organized life.

Unfortunately, the man next door appeared determined to test every promise she had made.

She watched him carry another box inside before catching herself staring.

“Get a grip, Lila,” she muttered.

Five minutes later, she was outside.

“Need a hand?” she called, approaching him with a confidence she hadn't entirely felt.

He turned.

His eyes were dark, steady, and unexpectedly warm. A slow smile spread across his face as he lowered the box.

“Depends. Are you actually offering help, or did you just come over to supervise?”

Lila laughed. “I haven't decided yet.”

“Then I suppose I'll have to give you a reason to stay.”

There was something about the way he said it that made her suddenly aware of the distance between them.

“I'm Lila Harper.”

“Darius Kane.”

His handshake was firm, his palm warm against hers. When their fingers separated, she found herself wishing the contact had lasted a little longer.

“So, Darius Kane,” she said, glancing at the boxes. “What brings you to our quiet little street?”

“Needed a change.”

“From what?”

He tilted his head. “That's a long story.”

“Good thing I like stories.”

“And what do you do when you're not interviewing your neighbors?”

“Marketing consultant. Occasional terrible cook. Full-time mind-your-own-business expert.”

“Interesting. You're not doing a very good job of that last one.”

She laughed again, and his smile deepened.

They worked together for another twenty minutes, exchanging stories and increasingly shameless teasing. Lila learned that Darius had recently left the city, worked in property development, and preferred quiet evenings to crowded clubs.

He learned that she lived alone, loved old movies, and had a weakness for men who knew how to make her laugh.

He did not ask whether she was single.

She did not volunteer the information.

Neither needed to.

When she reached for a smaller crate, her foot caught against the edge of a cardboard box. Darius steadied her by the elbow.

“You okay?”

“Perfectly fine.”

“Your balance suggests otherwise.”

“Perhaps you're distracting me.”

His smile faded into something more serious.

“Am I?”

Lila looked up at him. For a moment, the playful answer she had prepared disappeared.

“Yes,” she admitted.

The silence that followed felt different from the conversation before it. His hand remained at her elbow, gentle but reassuring, while she became acutely conscious of how close they were standing.

Then Darius released her.

“I should finish unpacking,” he said.

“Of course.”

She stepped back, annoyed by how much she wanted him to change his mind.

“Thanks for the help, Lila.”

“Anytime, neighbor.”

She returned to her house, determined not to look back.

She lasted exactly four seconds.

Darius was watching her from his driveway.

Their eyes met across the narrow strip of lawn.

He raised one hand in a small wave.

Lila shook her head, smiling despite herself, and disappeared inside.

That evening, she was halfway through a movie when her doorbell rang.

She opened the door to find Darius standing on her porch, wearing a fitted black T-shirt and holding an empty plate.

“I have a problem,” he announced.

“Already? You've been here less than a day.”

“My kitchen is a disaster, and I discovered that I own approximately twelve plates but absolutely no food.”

Lila folded her arms. “And you thought your best solution was to bother me?”

“I thought my best solution was to ask the prettiest woman on the street if she had anything edible.”

She tried not to smile.

“And if I say no?”

“Then I'll have to survive on bottled water and regret.”

She laughed and stepped aside.

“Come in, Darius. But if you insult my cooking, you're eating alone.”

He crossed the threshold, his shoulder brushing hers.

“I wouldn't dream of it.”

Neither of them noticed how naturally he settled into her living room, or how quickly their conversation turned from casual introductions to the kind of confessions people usually saved for much later.

When he finally stood to leave, it was nearly midnight.

At the door, he paused.

“I enjoyed tonight.”

“So did I.”

“Can I see you again?”

Lila looked at him for a long moment.

“Ask me tomorrow.”

He laughed softly. “You're going to make me work for this, aren't you?”

“Absolutely.”

He stepped onto the porch, then turned back.

“Good night, Lila.”

“Good night, Darius.”

She closed the door and leaned against it, smiling at the ceiling.

Her peaceful neighborhood had just become considerably more interesting.

And tomorrow, she suspected, would be even worse.

Or much, much better.
